worst_places.quote: Rules: (1) never hardcode secrets in workflow YAML; (2) never `echo` a secret value — GitHub automatically masks known secret values in logs but this is not foolproof; (3) use environment-level secrets (`environment: production`) for production credentials — these require approval before the job runs; (4) for third-party API keys, use OIDC (OpenID Connect) federated tokens instead of long-lived static keys when the provider supports it (AWS, GCP, Azure all do); (5) audit which workflows have access to which secrets.
worst_places.problem: 78 words in one sentence carrying five independent rules, three of them with their own em-dash caveat. On a phone this is a solid block with no line to stop on, and the reader has to hold five unrelated instructions in memory to reach the full stop. AWS, GCP and YAML are never expanded in this file. The RU twin (ru/09, same answer) is 75 words with the same shape, so the defect is in the source structure, not the translation.
worst_places.before: Rules: (1) never hardcode secrets in workflow YAML; (2) never `echo` a secret value — GitHub automatically masks known secret values in logs but this is not foolproof; (3) use environment-level secrets (`environment: production`) for production credentials — these require approval before the job runs; (4) for third-party API keys, use OIDC (OpenID Connect) federated tokens instead of long-lived static keys when the provider supports it (AWS, GCP, Azure all do); (5) audit which workflows have access to which secrets.
worst_places.after: Five rules. 1. Never hardcode a secret in the workflow YAML file. 2. Never `echo` a secret value. GitHub masks the secret values it knows about, but the mask is not foolproof. 3. For production credentials, use environment-level secrets (`environment: production`). A job that uses them waits for a human approval before it runs. 4. For third-party API keys, prefer OIDC (OpenID Connect) federated tokens over static keys that live forever. AWS (Amazon Web Services), GCP (Google Cloud Platform) and Azure all support this. 5. Audit which workflows can read which secrets.

worst_places.problem: The H1 of a fully Russian article is an English phrase — the same in 7 of 9 RU files (CI/CD Fundamentals, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Docker Essentials, Deployment Strategies, Environments and Configuration, Monitoring and Observability). This is not cosmetic: ru/08 cross-references this article 4 times as «См.: *[Основы CI/CD]*», a title that exists nowhere, and 5 of the 7 Russian names the RU glossary uses (Основы CI/CD, Основы Docker, Стратегии деплоя, Окружения и конфигурация, Мониторинг и наблюдаемость) match no heading. Meanwhile this same file's «Что дальше в этом разделе» block lists the siblings under a third set of names ([Docker Essentials], [Environments and Config], [CI/CD Glossary]). A Russian reader following a reference has two naming systems and neither resolves.

worst_places.quote: **Health check endpoint** — специальный API-маршрут в приложении, который сообщает, является ли сервис здоровым и готовым принимать трафик. Это не пользовательская функция — это инфраструктурная сантехника.
worst_places.problem: «инфраструктурная сантехника» is a word-for-word calque of "infrastructure plumbing". In Russian «сантехника» means bathroom fixtures, so the sentence reads as a typo and the metaphor carries none of the English meaning ("unglamorous machinery nobody looks at"). The reader stops, re-reads, and gets nothing. The same sentence also uses the bureaucratic «является ли сервис здоровым» where «здоров ли сервис» is the natural Russian.

worst_places.quote: Logging PII or credentials is a security/compliance violation (GDPR, PCI DSS, HIPAA — different regulatory frameworks, all require protecting user data).
worst_places.problem: Three regulation acronyms are dropped on the reader unexpanded, plus "compliance" as an unglossed noun and the slash construction "security/compliance". The RU version of this exact line expands all three («GDPR — Общий регламент защиты данных ЕС, PCI DSS — стандарт безопасности платёжных карт, HIPAA — закон о медицинских данных США»), so here the EN reader is handed strictly less than the RU reader. The EN glossary does not have GDPR-adjacent entries for PCI DSS's parts either (CVV, CCPA, HIPAA appear inside definitions unexpanded).
worst_places.before: Logging PII or credentials is a security/compliance violation (GDPR, PCI DSS, HIPAA — different regulatory frameworks, all require protecting user data).
worst_places.after: Logging PII or credentials breaks both your security rules and the law. Three regulations matter here: GDPR (the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation), PCI DSS (the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) and HIPAA (the US law covering health data). They cover different areas, but every one of them requires you to protect user data.

worst_places.quote: **Infrastructure as Code** (IaC — pronounced "eye-ack") is the practice of defining and managing infrastructure — servers, networks, databases, load balancers, DNS records — in code files (typically YAML, JSON, or a domain-specific language) rather than by clicking through a web console or running manual shell commands.
worst_places.problem: 44 words. Between the subject and the end of the definition the reader passes a parenthesis, a five-item em-dash insertion, a second parenthesis with three more items, and only then reaches the contrast "rather than". The one thing the sentence is for — IaC means writing code instead of clicking — arrives last. DNS and YAML are unexpanded. The RU twin is 42 words with the same shape.
worst_places.before: **Infrastructure as Code** (IaC — pronounced "eye-ack") is the practice of defining and managing infrastructure — servers, networks, databases, load balancers, DNS records — in code files (typically YAML, JSON, or a domain-specific language) rather than by clicking through a web console or running manual shell commands.
worst_places.after: **Infrastructure as Code** (IaC — pronounced "eye-ack") means describing your infrastructure in code files instead of clicking through a web console or typing shell commands by hand. "Infrastructure" here means servers, networks, databases, load balancers and DNS records (Domain Name System — the records that map a domain name to a server). The code files are usually YAML, JSON, or a language built specifically for the tool.

worst_places.problem: This line sits inside a single-stage Dockerfile (one `FROM node:20-alpine`) in the "Non-root user" section, but copies from a stage named `builder` that only exists in the multi-stage example two sections earlier. Copy-pasted as printed, it fails with `invalid from flag value builder`. The next snippet in the same section ("Simpler approach using the built-in node user") repeats the mistake. worst_places.before:
FROM node:20-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./

worst_places.after:
# Stage 1 — build, so this file runs on its own
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2 — the image we ship
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist

patterns: Domain terms are defined with real care; everything imported from the surrounding ecosystem is treated as common vocabulary. Every article patiently builds up pipeline, job, step, artifact, runner, layer, span, probe, error budget — and in the same paragraph drops AWS, EC2, S3, ECR, ECS, VPC, IAM, ALB, RDS, AMI, CDN, TLS, DNS, TTL, SDK, W3C, PID, UID, YAML with no expansion. The author expanded what the article is *about* and skipped every acronym that merely passes through. This is the single highest-value fix in the zone and it is mechanical: 269 flagged first-uses, of which roughly two thirds are genuine.

A transliteration layer sits on top of otherwise living Russian, and it is inconsistent with itself. Invented words: «аутаджи» (outages), «деплоябельный», «мелкогранулярный», «дрейнировать», «мониторируемый», «коллаборанты», «перезаклонировать», «лаунчер», «консьюмеры», «скрейпит», «предсозданный». Mistranslation repeated as a section heading 5 times: «Старший нюанс» for "Senior nuance". Dead calqued metaphor: «инфраструктурная сантехника». And the same English term gets 2-3 different Russian renderings across files: «три столпа» / «три кита» (three pillars), «проба живучести» / «проба живости» (liveness probe), «гранулированный» / «мелкогранулярный» (fine-grained), «аудируемо» / «аудитируемость». A reader moving between articles cannot tell these are the same concept.

`09-*-interview-questions.md` is the structural outlier in both locales and needs its own pass. 4500-5200 words, 41 over-long paragraphs, 17% over-long sentences in EN (up to 78 words), and one code block in the whole file. Its signature habit is packing 3-6 enumerated facts into a single sentence as "(1)…(2)…(3)…" — six answers do this. Every other file in the zone interrupts theory with a diagram or code block every 2-3 paragraphs; this one runs 68 paragraphs without a break, in the file a candidate is most likely to read end-to-end on a phone.

Untranslated H1s in 7 of 9 RU files have broken the RU locale's internal navigation. The RU glossary points at articles by Russian names (Основы CI/CD, Основы Docker, Стратегии деплоя, Окружения и конфигурация, Мониторинг и наблюдаемость) that match no heading, while ru/01's own 'what's next' block points at the same articles by their English names. Two incompatible naming systems inside one locale, neither of which resolves.
notes:
Zone question — no, the glossary does not excuse the other eight files, and it could not even if it were linked: it omits VM, PR, MR, TLS, CDN, SDK, IAM, JWT, S3, EC2, OS, UID, SHA, SaaS, CLI, UI, which the other files use unexpanded. No file links to it at an acronym's first use; only 01 mentions it once in a 'what's next' block. The glossary itself reads well as reference prose (C=5: every entry leads with its definition) but is a 107-paragraph wall with 51-62 over-long paragraphs and zero diagrams or tables, and has 4 dangling cross-references — *Span*, *Sidecar*, *Exec form* and *Monitoring* are pointed at but have no entries in either locale.
Outside my remit but it blocks comprehension: en/07 L568 and ru/07 L570 say a *readiness* probe checking external dependencies causes pod restarts; the anti-pattern section 150 lines earlier correctly says *liveness*, and 09 words the same trap correctly. A reader who noticed the first version will not trust either.
Small mechanical defects: ru/07 «SLI пропускной сп.:количество» (missing space), ru/02 «упакованных в одну вызов», ru/08 «CloudFormation создаёт ими управляет» (missing «и»). en/08's cross-reference *[Environments and Config]* does not match that article's H1 'Environments and Configuration'.
The verdict is systemic-refactor rather than targeted-fixes because two of seven criteria (A 2.9, G 2.7) fail across all 18 / all 9 RU files with one shared root cause each — not because the depth or structure is wrong. B/C/D/E are genuinely strong (3.5-4.6); the ASCII diagrams and the definition-first section openings are the best thing in this zone and should be left alone.
